extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, law students, and courts handling patent license disputes
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing patent licenses: their effect on ability to challenge patent validity (estoppel), consideration and royalties, forfeiture and remedies for breach, transferability/assignability, and implied licenses arising from sales or dealings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee estopped from denying patent validity while exercising license
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee, having accepted and while exercising the rights conferred by a license, is estopped from denying the validity of the patent in any suit in which such exercise of his license privileges is the basis of the controversy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the license admits the validity of the patent, or provides that no act shall impair that admission, the licensee cannot at any time during the period for which the license was granted attack the patent. Cases: Woodworth v. Cook (1850); White v. Lee (1882); Brown v. Lapham (1886); Baltimore Car Wheel Co. v. North Baltimore Passenger Ry. Co. (1884). Exceptions and nuances: a license avoided for breach of condition may restore parties to original rights; a licensee who repudiates his license may cease claiming its protection and thereafter may defend on the ground that the patent is invalid (see discussion on repudiation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender by one joint-licensee does not affect others
rubrics_metrics.description: The surrender of a license by one of several joint-licensees does not affect the privileges of the others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surrender by part of the licensees does not avoid the license as to the remaining licensees. (Cases e.g., Thebenth v. Celluloid Mfg. Co. (1880)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlimited, unconditioned license is irrevocable
rubrics_metrics.description: A license unlimited as to time and not conditioned otherwise than on the grant of the patent is irrevocable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Kelly v. Porter (1883) and related authority. A license paid for by a gross sum in advance and not conditional is generally irrevocable unless explicitly provided otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignor/assignee license estoppel
rubrics_metrics.description: An assignor taking a license under his assignee is estopped to deny the validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Consolidated Middlings Purifier Co. v. Guilder (1881) and other cited cases. The doctrine prevents an assignor who accepts benefits under a license from later disputing the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purchaser from licensee not estopped to deny validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A purchaser from the licensee is not estopped to deny the validity of the patent in an infringement suit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Baltimore Car Wheel Co. v. North Baltimore Passenger Ry. Co. (1884) illustrates that transferees/purchasers do not automatically inherit the licensee's estoppel to deny validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamping/articles labeling by licensee constitutes admission
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee stamping articles with the name and date of the patent thereby admits that they were made under the protection of his license and is estopped as to those articles from disputing the validity of the patent or his obligations to the licensor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Jones v. Vankirk (1865) and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration for license may be money or other objects; forms of payment
rubrics_metrics.description: The consideration for a license, moving from the licensee to the licensor, may be money or any other object or obligation; monetary consideration may be payable as a gross sum (advance or deferred), periodic instalments, or amounts determined by extent of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The parties can structure payment as they agree; gross-advance payments often affect revocability; periodic royalties raise different questions about revocability and remedies. (See §821 and cited cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of gross advance payment on revocability
rubrics_metrics.description: When the license is paid for by a gross sum in advance and not upon condition, it is irrevocable (absent an express reservation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Wood v. Wells, Crittenden & Co. (1878). By contrast, payment by periodic royalties does not by itself alter questions of revocability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for royalties while benefiting from license; duty to demand
rubrics_metrics.description: A licensee is liable for royalties while he takes the benefit of any of the patents covered by his license and remains liable until evicted; it is ordinarily the duty of the licensor to demand royalties rather than merely wait for payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Licensee's liability persists until eviction; failure to pay may support actions at law for recovery and equitable rescission proceedings. (Pope Mfg. Co. v. Owsley; McKay v. Jackman; White v. Lee).

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty timing and calculation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Royalties may be fixed per article, based on number sold/made, payable quarterly or otherwise; agreements specifying payment timing determine when royalties become due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: if royalties are payable quarterly and license executed Jan 7, first royalty payable Apr 1 (Dare v. Boylston (1880)). An agreement to pay royalties up to a certain amount within a specified time may obligate absolute payment of that amount; other royalties accruing later are additional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royalty collectible only if patent has value (practising vs selling)
rubrics_metrics.description: On a license to practise the invention (as distinguished from selling), the royalty is not collectible if the patent is worthless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Jenkins v. Abbotts (1874); distinction between licenses to use/practice and to sell is material to collectibility of royalties when patent is invalidated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement not to deny validity can be enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: An agreement or covenant by the licensee not to set up the invalidity of the patent as a defense may be enforced in many circumstances and will prevail in some cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Heilner v. Battin (1856) and other authorities show courts may enforce explicit covenants not to contest validity; but there are limits and equity principles may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights to royalties are property and insurable
rubrics_metrics.description: A right to royalties is property and is insurable like other property; the owner of royalties has an insurable interest in the factory where the articles are made, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National Filtering Oil Co. v. Citizens Insurance Co. (1885) and other cases recognize royalties as property interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies for non-payment: actions at law and equity rescission
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to make stipulated payments renders the licensee liable to an action at law to recover them and to a proceeding in equity for rescission of the license; equity, however, will often avoid immediate forfeiture and proceed to rescission or damages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although early doctrine treated any breach as automatic forfeiture, modern courts require express forfeiture stipulations or will exercise equitable powers to avoid harsh ipso facto forfeiture; remedies include damages or equitable rescission followed by infringement suits. (See §822 and cited cases including Hartwell v. Tilghman).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express stipulation required for immediate ipso facto forfeiture in many cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts now generally require an express stipulation in the license that it shall be forfeited upon breach before treating a mere breach (e.g., non-payment) as causing ipso facto forfeiture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To avoid oppressive outcomes and multiplicity of issues, modern decisions modify the old doctrine that any breach worked forfeiture; licenses remain pleadable until rescinded by a court of equity if not expressly declared forfeitable. (See §822 discussion and cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity's approach to rescission for breach
rubrics_metrics.description: In equity, rescission of a license for breach (such as non-payment) is governed by ordinary equitable principles; tender or subsequent payment may prevent rescission if justice can be done by damages or payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts consider whether justice can be done by judgment for amount due; tender after default may cure a forfeiture provision (Dare v. Boylston). Equity will consider whether breaches indicate likely future non-payment or other injuries before annulling license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-payment plus abandonment or hostile conduct can justify rescission
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-payment of royalties coupled with abandonment of license privileges, conduct causing other injuries to the licensor, or circumstances indicating future non-payment may be grounds for equity to annul the license and restore original rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity examines the totality of circumstances; mere non-payment is less likely to produce rescission when curable, but abandonment/repudiation or conduct hostile to the patent may justify annulment (cases cited in §822).

rubrics_metrics.name: Repudiation severs licensee/licensor relations and treats later acts as infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: Open repudiation of the license by words or conduct severs relations; from that time the licensor may treat the licensee's acts within the patent scope as infringements and the licensee cannot plead the license as a defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repudiation is more than a ground of forfeiture; it authorizes the licensor to enforce monopoly rights immediately. Cases: Pope Mfg. Co. v. Owsley; Magic Ruffle Co. v. Elm City Co.; others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer to take a license does not estop offeror from denying validity
rubrics_metrics.description: An offer to take a license does not estop the offeror from denying the validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evans v. Eaton (1816) and other cases make clear mere offers are insufficient to create estoppel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expired license does not bar denial of patent validity
rubrics_metrics.description: An expired license is no bar to the denial of the validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blatherwick v. Carey (1881) and similar cases show estoppel tied to the continuing effect of the license; once expired, the licensee (or others) may challenge validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transferability/assignability depends on parties' intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a license is transferable depends on the intention of the parties: licenses are not assignable unless it affirmatively appears that such was the intention; words like 'and his assigns' are qualified where the rights conferred are evidently not transferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look to license language, nature of transaction, consideration paid, and surrounding circumstances. (Dorsey Revolving Harvester Rake Co. v. Bradley Mfg. Co.; other cited authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Personal/use-at-shop licenses are not assignable
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to use 'in the licensee's own business' or 'at his shop' is personal and cannot be assigned; similarly 'shop-right' licenses are personal and nonassignable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eclipse Windmill Co. v. Woodmanse Windmill Co.; Gibbs v. Hoefner; other cases. Such personal licenses usually do not pass to receivers or successors absent express provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licenses to use for specified quantity/gross-sum payments are prima facie assignable
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to use to a certain quantity on payment of a gross sum is prima facie assignable, because it makes no difference to the licensor by whom the quantity is used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include licenses for a specified quantity per year paid as a gross sum (Belding v. Turner and related cases). The specific terms and intent can rebut the prima facie assignability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partnership and death effects on licenses
rubrics_metrics.description: A license to a partnership is not affected by a change of members unless the license otherwise provides; an exclusive right granted to a licensee vests at his death in his personal representatives so far as needed to finish devices on hand, but generally personal licenses do not pass to a receiver.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Belding v. Turner; Pitts v. Jameson; Curran v. Craig; other cases explain how licenses operate with respect to partners, retirement, death, and receiverships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized transfer may be ratified by acceptance of royalties from assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: An unauthorized assignment/transfer of a license may be validated or ratified by the licensor's acceptance of royalties or license-fees from the assignee after notice of the assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance of payments can be evidence of ratification unless the licensor shows contrary intent (Wilde v. Smith; Bloomer v. Gilpin).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied licenses from lawful sale or dealings
rubrics_metrics.description: The law may imply a license from the dealings of the parties or from a lawful sale of a patented article—e.g., licenses implied in favor of a purchaser at any lawful sale of a patented article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: §824 introduces the doctrine that certain dealings imply a license; the seller's rights and limitations, and the nature of the sale, determine the scope of any implied license. (The page begins this discussion; additional detail appears beyond this chunk.)
